title: Preventing Cross-Site Scripting
learning_outcomes: Explain how Preventing Cross-Site Scripting relates to React Security and Privacy.
Apply Rendering untrusted text in a small React or JavaScript example and describe the expected result.
Test one edge/failure case and identify a maintainable, accessible fix.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study Preventing Cross-Site Scripting as part of React Security and Privacy. The syllabus topics are kept below, then connected to a small example you can inspect and adapt.
content.why_it_matters: Rendering untrusted text is part of a trust boundary. Treat browser input and client state as untrusted; enforce authorization, validation, and secrets on the server, then provide clear UI feedback.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Rendering untrusted text is part of a trust boundary. Treat browser input and client state as untrusted; enforce authorization, validation, and secrets on the server, then provide clear UI feedback. Start with one responsibility at a time: identify the data, describe the expected interface, then decide which event, state update, request, or runtime boundary changes the result.

content.task: Create a minimal example demonstrating Preventing Cross-Site Scripting. Include the relevant subtopic “Rendering untrusted text”, explain the expected UI/result, and verify one normal case plus one boundary or failure case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates the named concept rather than merely mentioning it.
The expected visible or logged result is documented and reproducible.
At least one boundary, empty, loading, or failure case is handled or explained.
The implementation remains accessible and does not introduce avoidable mutation, stale state, or insecure client-only trust.
hints: Start with the smallest part of “Rendering untrusted text” that can be observed independently.
Write down what should appear before changing the code; then change one input at a time.
Use the browser console, React Developer Tools, or the appropriate test/runtime to isolate a mismatch.
content.expected_output: The name is rendered as text through JSX; privileged HTML injection is avoided.

common_mistakes.problem: The example handles only the happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Real UI receives empty values, delayed responses, and invalid input.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one explicit edge/failure case and document the expected message or state.

common_mistakes.problem: The example stores redundant data or mutates an existing array/object.
common_mistakes.why: The displayed result can drift from the source data or React may not observe the intended change.
common_mistakes.fix: Derive values where possible and create a new value when updating state.

common_mistakes.problem: A browser or framework capability is assumed to exist everywhere.
common_mistakes.why: Availability can depend on the host runtime, React version, and framework.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the official reference, declare the runtime/version, and provide a fallback when appropriate.
